analysis.one_liner: Expands Pell Grants and college transparency, paid for by repealing 2017 tax breaks for high earners and large estates.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on October 11, 2019 with zero cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have roughly doubled the maximum federal Pell Grant to $10,000 and expanded the pool of low-income students who automatically qualify for the maximum award. It would have paid for this by repealing two 2017 tax-law benefits that go mainly to wealthy households: the higher alternative minimum tax exemption and the doubled estate and gift tax exemption. It also would have pressured states to keep funding public colleges and forced colleges to publish graduation, salary, and debt data.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income college students and their families. The bill would have raised the maximum Pell Grant to $10,000 for the 2019-20 school year with annual inflation increases after that, and would have let families earning up to 250% of the poverty line automatically qualify for a zero expected family contribution on a shortened financial aid form. Students would also have gained standardized public data on graduation rates broken out by income, race, and first-generation status, graduate salaries, and average debt, making it easier to judge whether a college is worth the price. States and colleges that serve students well would benefit from continued Pell funding tied to state maintenance of effort.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the maximum federal Pell Grant to $10,000 for the 2019-20 award year, with the amount adjusted upward each year after that, roughly doubling the award from its prior level.

Expands the automatic zero expected family contribution to any family with income at or below 250% of the poverty line, and creates a simplified financial aid application requiring less data from those families, so more low-income students qualify for the maximum grant without a lengthy paperwork process.

Bars colleges in states that cut higher education funding below their 10-year average from receiving Pell Grant dollars, aiming to stop states from shifting college costs onto students while federal aid fills the gap.

Requires every college taking federal aid to post on its homepage a standard set of performance indicators: graduation rates disaggregated by income, race, and first-generation status, average salary three years after graduation, employment in the field of study, average debt at graduation and at withdrawal, net price by income quartile, and a two-question student satisfaction survey.
Directs the Education Department to help colleges with fewer than 5,000 students pay for the new data collection, with the per-student data fee raised from $5 to $6 for those schools.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy households and large estates would bear the cost: the bill repeals the increased alternative minimum tax exemption (effective after 2018) and moves up the expiration of the doubled estate and gift tax exemption from 2026 to enactment, using that revenue for Pell Grants. States that have reduced higher education funding would face a choice between restoring funding and losing Pell Grants for their institutions. Colleges would bear the cost of collecting and publishing the new performance data, though small colleges get federal help with it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy households, large estates, and colleges

drawbacks.text: Repealing the increased alternative minimum tax exemption raises taxes not only on the very wealthy but on households in high-tax states that get caught by the AMT, some of them upper-middle-income rather than rich, so the funding mechanism lands on a broader group than just millionaires.

The state maintenance-of-effort penalty is blunt: if a state fails to keep higher education funding at its 10-year average, every college in that state loses Pell eligibility, which cuts off aid for the very students the bill is meant to help rather than penalizing the state government directly.

The performance-disclosure mandate imposes new reporting and data-collection duties on colleges, and while the bill provides assistance to small institutions, larger colleges would absorb the compliance cost themselves, and metrics like average graduate salary can disadvantage schools serving lower-income regions or fields like teaching and the arts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: doubling the Pell Grant and widening automatic eligibility would substantially cut the debt burden of the lowest-income students, and the disclosure requirements give prospective students real information for free. The costs fall mostly on people with the most ability to pay, which was the point. The two honest weaknesses are the AMT repeal's reach beyond the truly wealthy and a state-funding penalty whose enforcement mechanism would punish students in the states with the worst budget cuts. On balance, a well-aimed bill whose main design risk is collateral damage from its enforcement tool.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees in October 2019, neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on October 11, 2019, and the Speaker referred it to the Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, since it touched both education programs and tax law.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with a single sponsor from introduction to the end of the Congress.
Neither committee held a hearing, marked up the bill, or reported it out, and it never reached the House floor for a vote.
The bill died automatically on January 3, 2021, when the 116th Congress ended, as do all bills not enacted by the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy households and large estates kept the 2017 tax exemptions the bill would have repealed, and colleges avoided the new performance-disclosure requirements. Low-income students gained nothing; no member of the House besides the sponsor pushed the bill at any point.

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Education and Labor and Ways and Means committees; found no cosponsors and no committee took it up.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the tax-writing committee that would have had to act on its revenue provisions.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in the committee with jurisdiction over Pell Grants and college aid.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; it had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have repealed the higher AMT exemption and moved up the sunset of the doubled estate and gift tax exemption, directly raising taxes on these households to fund student aid. Their gain from the bill's death was keeping those tax benefits.

Institutions would have gained continued federal Pell dollars conditioned on state funding, but would have had to publish detailed graduation, salary, debt, and satisfaction data, which hurts schools whose outcomes look bad once visible. Schools in states that cut higher education funding risked losing Pell eligibility entirely.
